transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-12-20
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Liam (Redwood SE), Noah (Redwood SE), Rachel (Starlight CISO), Daniel (Starlight SecOps), Priya (Starlight Cloud)

Auto-generated Summary:
Quick review of audit logging capabilities, what admin actions are captured, export mechanisms to SIEM, retention options and encryption/KMS integration. Customer asked about retention windows, immutability, and proof for audits.

Topics:
- What events are logged (admin/admin UI/console/API/token/key ops)
- Export options (S3 push, syslog, webhook, SIEM connector)
- Retention and custom retention per tenant
- KMS/HSM integration for logs and audit proofing
- RBAC/SSO admin activity audit trails and user identity mapping

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone thanks for joining, uh today we're going to walk through audit logs and admin activity capture in Redwood, and cover export, retention, encryption. You all got the deck?
[00:08] Rachel: Yep we've got it. Thanks Maya. High level we need to validate this for a boards audit and our SOC 2 evidentiary checklist.
[00:15] Maya: Great, that's exactly what we'll focus on. Liam, can you kick off with what we capture by default?
[00:20] Liam: Sure. So by default Redwood captures three categories - control plane admin events, user API events and system events. Control plane admin events are things like user creation, role changes, SSO config updates, API key lifecycle, and dedicated capacity changes. API events include generation requests, embeddings calls, model selection, but the payload is redacted by default (we keep metadata not content). System events are infra-level like node restarts, autoscale events, and failed deploys.
[00:45] Rachel: Quick question: do you capture the full prompt or any PII in logs?
[00:50] Liam: We do not capture full prompt content in audit logs by default; request/response bodies are excluded from the admin audit stream. We emit metadata: request id, model name, token counts, latency, redwood-region, and user id/email. If customers opt-in for deeper debugging audits there's a separate debug trace flow but that is off by default and requires explicit consent and retention controls.
[01:10] Priya: When you say user id/email, is that the identity from SSO/SAML? We need mapping to our AD identities.
[01:16] Noah: Yes, we map SSO principals—SAML or OIDC—to the internal user id. Logs include both the SSO principal and internal role at time of event so you can tie actions back to your AD account. Sometimes the auto-parse has name mismatches but you get the external_id field.
[01:33] Daniel: For audit we need immutability for 1 year, and we forward to our SIEM (Splunk). Does Redwood support push to S3 or push to syslog or direct splunk forwarders?
[01:45] Liam: We have multiple export options. Out of box you can configure an S3 export which is append-only and supports server-side encryption with your KMS keys. We also support push to your HTTPS endpoint or a webhook, syslog via a connector, and a direct Splunk HEC integration (we've seen customers use both HEC and S3). We can also stream via Kafka if you want a pull model.
[02:05] Rachel: For regulatory evidence we need an audit trail that can't be tampered with. Does S3 export provide versioning/immutability?
[02:12] Maya: We recommend S3 with object lock enabled and a retention policy on your bucket. On Redwood side exports are write-once per file; we don't allow shallow edits to previously exported files. If you need legal hold we suggest the S3 object lock and your own bucket so you control immutability.
[02:30] Priya: How long do you keep logs on Redwood side? Our default policy is 90 days, but we might require 2 years for certain data classes.
[02:38] Liam: By default we retain audit logs 90 days in the hosted control plane. For enterprise/private we support extended retention up to configurable windows per account—30 days up to 7 years—depending on contract and storage add-on. You can also set per-tenant retention policies. Note there are cost and compliance tradeoffs; longer retention is possible when you host the exports in your bucket.
[03:00] Daniel: Any previews for retention in the console?
[03:03] Noah: Yes, the audit log page includes filters and a retention indicator. You can run exports for arbitrary windows. The UI supports continuity search and you can pull CSV/NDJSON exports.
[03:15] Rachel: On encryption—we require logs to be encrypted with our KMS and keys rotated annually. Is there a way to use our KMS?
[03:23] Liam: Yes, we support customer-managed keys. For hosted we have KMS integrations with AWS KMS and GCP KMS for exports to your buckets; we can also integrate with your HSM for on-prem/private deployments. The control plane metadata is encrypted at rest, and for export we can sign objects with your key. Key rotation is supported—Redwood doesn't delete older objects during rotation, we rotate new object encryption.
[03:45] Priya: What about log integrity proofs—do you do signing or a hash chain?
[03:50] Liam: We currently provide SHA256 checksums for exported bundles and an append-only manifest that you can store. We also offer an optional signed digest service for enterprise customers that signs daily manifests with an HSM-backed key. That's on our enterprise security add-on.
[04:08] Rachel: Good. For internal reviews, we need to show who changed RBAC roles and when. What granularity do you capture for role changes and policy updates?
[04:18] Liam: Role changes include actor identity, old/new role, resource scope, timestamp, and API call id. Policy updates show the diff where possible, and we store previous policy text for up to the configured retention period. We also capture why if a reason field is provided during the change.
[04:36] Daniel: How do you handle service accounts vs human users in the logs? We need to separate machine principals from people.
[04:41] Noah: We tag principals with type: human or service. Service accounts have additional metadata: service id, owning team, and token id. You can filter on principal.type in the audit viewer.
[04:52] Priya: When you integrate with our SIEM do you preserve the JSON schema so we can map fields? We use a standard Splunk sourcetype.
[04:58] Liam: Yes exports are NDJSON with stable field names. We include a schema doc and a sample mapping to Splunk HEC. For the syslog connector we flatten fields and include a sourcetype header you can set. We can also provide a Grok pattern if needed.
[05:13] Rachel: Is there a way to stream alerts for specific admin events? Like role escalations or API key creation?
[05:19] Maya: Yes, you can configure audit alerts in the console—push to webhook, pager duty, or SNS. You can select event types and severity thresholds.
[05:28] Daniel: For our compliance team, we need to periodically export evidence for auditor review. Is there an automated export job?
[05:34] Liam: You can schedule exports daily/weekly and have them written to your S3 bucket with optional encryption and hashed manifests. We can also generate an auditor-friendly report that summarizes RBAC changes, admin logins, and unusual patterns for a given period.
[05:48] Priya: About the debug traces you mentioned earlier—if we enable them for a short window, how do you ensure PII is masked?
[05:55] Noah: Debug traces are gated behind an access control and must be explicitly consented. We support field-level redaction rules and can run redaction at export time. For regulated customers we recommend doing traces in a private deployment or using an isolated debug bucket.
[06:10] Rachel: Ok, question on private deployments: if we run Redwood Private in our VPC, do audit logs stay inside our network?
[06:16] Liam: Yes. For Private deployments audit logs can be written to your internal object store or forwarded to your SIEM without leaving your VPC. Control plane metadata can be run in your private control plane as well. Key management stays with you.
[06:28] Daniel: Any limitation on event volume or throttling when streaming to SIEM? We have peaks during batch runs.
[06:34] Liam: We handle burst buffering and backpressure. For high-volume customers we recommend using the Kafka stream model or S3 exports to blunt spikes. The direct HEC forwarder has reasonable throughput but if you anticipate sustained high qps we usually configure batching and retries and discuss rate limits in the SOW.
[06:52] Priya: For vendor attestations—can we get a signed SOC 2 report and pen test summary?
[06:58] Maya: Yes, we'll share our SOC 2 Type II report and the latest penetration test summary. I'll attach them to the ticket.
[07:05] Rachel: Good. A couple of edge items: we need to know retention per environment (staging vs prod), and whether the exported files include the internal user id mapping table.
[07:15] Liam: You can configure retention per environment; exported bundles include the mapping table as optional metadata. The mapping table can be excluded if you want hash-only mapping for privacy.
[07:28] Daniel: For timeline, we want to run a 2-week pilot in January with exports to our Splunk, validate immutability, and run a compliance checklist. What do you need from us?
[07:36] Maya: We'll need a staging account, your Splunk HEC endpoint and token, the SIEM sourcetype you'd like, and the KMS key ARN if you want us to test encryption. We'll also schedule a short walkthrough on the export flow.
[07:48] Priya: We'll get those over after this call. Also want a short demo of the RBAC audit UI—can we do that in the pilot?
[07:55] Noah: Absolutely—demo and a hands-on session.
[08:00] Rachel: Perfect. Anything else on logs themselves?
[08:03] Liam: One small note—sensitive fields are hashed by default in the NDJSON export; if you need full text debug it's a separate gated flow.
[08:12] Maya: Ok let's recap next steps and owners.
[08:16] Maya: Action items: I'll send SOC 2 and schema; Liam will send KMS guide; Priya will share retention and endpoints; Daniel will confirm hold windows. We'll set up pilot kickoff for week of Jan 4.
[08:28] Rachel: Sounds good thanks everyone.
[08:30] Maya: Thanks, end of call.
